children.text: The GB10 in my ASUS Ascent GX10 shares one memory pool between the CPU and GPU, as the NVIDIA DGX Spark does. A large model load can therefore consume memory the host needs for services such as SSH. In my tests, running out of headroom did not always produce a clean allocation failure: the machine could stop responding.

That happened three times in July 2026. Each incident lasted 35 to 65 minutes and ended with a power cycle. I built a guard to stop a workload before the host reaches that state. This post explains the failures, the measurements behind the guard, and the limits of the protection. The scripts are in
This account concerns one GX10 installation. The repository records Ubuntu, kernel
, systemd, cgroup v2, and Docker as the tested environment. The implementation described here is pinned to
. Behavior on another kernel, driver, or container runtime needs its own check.
The successful over-commit tests used a 4 GiB hard floor and a 1 GiB
setting. The current defaults are 3 GiB and 256 MiB. That distinction matters: the tests support the approach, but do not validate those newer defaults.
On 2026-07-01 I started Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (NVFP4) in vLLM with

body.code: NVRM: GPU0 nvCheckOkFailedNoLog: Check failed: Out of memory [NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY] ... _memdescAllocInternal(pMemDesc) @ mem_desc.c:1336

The kernel was still producing hung-task reports while normal services stopped making progress. Those symptoms were consistent with a memory-reclaim livelock, although the logs alone do not establish every part of the failure mechanism. With
, and no watchdog configured, this installation had no automatic recovery path for the observed hang.

The kernel OOM killer and earlyoom both failed to stop the workload in time. SSH, which I needed to intervene, was also unusable.
The kernel OOM killer ran, but its victims included

at about 32 MB of resident memory (RSS), far below the memory I attributed to the GPU workload. That discrepancy helps explain the poor victim selection; RSS was not a reliable measure of this workload's total impact on the host.

17:21:21 earlyoom: mem avail:     0 of 124546 MiB ( 0.00%), swap free: 13233 of 16383 MiB (80.77%)

The kernel's OOM report from 07-01 shows the problem in one place:

use a different unit. At 4 KiB per page on this installation, the listed anonymous, file, shared-memory, and unreclaimable-slab counts total about 1.8 GiB. The excerpt shows very little free memory in the Normal zone and an

My working explanation was that the model load left too little headroom for the host. vLLM's

is a budget based on GPU-visible memory; on this machine the host shares the same physical pool. Loading weights, profiling, repacking, and allocating the KV cache can also create peaks that a steady-state fit estimate misses. The logs establish severe allocation pressure, but they do not isolate the contribution of every loading phase.
How much memory a model actually gets
on my GX10. That is the useful starting point for a host-memory budget. My accounting from
and the boot log puts roughly 6.5 GiB outside that total:
0.37 GiB is never handed to Linux by the firmware.
3.55 GiB is reserved by firmware before Linux starts. One block of 2.56 GiB is the largest;
array, 64 bytes of bookkeeping for every 4 KiB page.
About 0.45 GiB for the kernel image and early boot allocations.

These are rounded figures from this installation, not a universal GB10 memory map. A model must fit alongside the operating system, runtime, KV cache, and temporary allocations. Checkpoint size on disk is only a starting estimate: quantization, loading strategy, and offloading change the resident footprint.

In that run, the growth in

The guard uses this alternative signal, with all inputs converted to bytes:

For a reproducible calculation, use all three fields from one /proc/meminfo snapshot and convert them to the same unit. Rounded values gathered at different times cannot establish an exact headroom figure.
To inspect the inputs on another machine, capture them together while the workload is running:

Two more details matter for anything that measures memory on a GB10:

llama.cpp behaved differently in an October 19 run:
stayed near 0.3 GiB while the server was active, and its memory appeared as ordinary used memory. The large

increase came after exit. I have not isolated why the engines differed. The same guard formula remains usable in this case because subtracting the small non-slab component changes little, but it is not an independent validation of the estimate.
, a Python daemon using only the standard library. It aims to sample
and its recent fall rate, and applies three rules. These are the current defaults; the stress-test results later in this post used an older hard floor.
If headroom is falling faster than 2 GiB/s and its recent rate projects a drop below 3 GiB within 0.5 s, send SIGKILL.
is below 3 GiB, send SIGKILL without waiting for the soft threshold.
After 2 s accumulated below 8 GiB in one low-memory episode, send SIGTERM. Escalate to SIGKILL after 10 s if the target is still present and the episode has not recovered.
The scan looks for Docker scopes containing a command line with
. It orders matching scopes by their filesystem modification time, using that as a proxy for the newest workload. This is a selection policy, not a measurement of which workload caused the pressure.

During a vLLM load the KV cache allocation drains memory at 17 to 41 GiB/s in my tests, and a killed process takes seconds to give memory back. A rule based only on the level has to sit around 20 GiB to survive that, which is what an early version did, and it kept a sixth of the machine unusable. Projecting the current rate 0.5 s ahead catches the ramp early while still letting a steady workload run closer to the floor.

The 0.5 s horizon is a tuning choice informed by two observed post-kill drops: 0.6 GiB and 14.6 GiB. Sending a signal does not immediately release every allocation, particularly when work remains blocked in the kernel or driver. A longer horizon would intervene earlier but also stop more loads that could have completed. These observations do not prove that 0.5 s covers every overshoot.
This rule has a cost I should be clear about: it fires when
drops under 3 GiB. A vLLM load still allocating at 17 GiB/s is killed once headroom falls below about 11.5 GiB. A config whose KV allocation would finish with 6 GiB free does not survive the load.
Why the slow rule has hysteresis

Replaying 2.5 days of recordings showed 116 crossings of the 8 GiB line. A workload hovering around that threshold kept resetting the old timers. The current episode starts when a rule trips and ends when headroom reaches at least 9 GiB and the ramp rule is clear. Only time actually spent below the soft threshold counts toward its 2 s dwell. In the replay, 116 crossings became 9 episodes.

The 10 s escalation interval also came from logs: clean exits after SIGTERM took 0.5 to 7.6 s in the observed runs. I use 10 s as a practical cutoff for this workload, rather than a general bound on how long shutdown should take.
How it kills, and why not through Docker

An early version used the Docker API to kill containers. During a severe pressure test, that call timed out after 3 s and the exception crashed the guard. systemd restarted it twice while the headroom estimate went negative. The machine recovered, but the incident showed why the kill path should not depend on a responsive Docker daemon.
Target discovery and signalling now use cgroups and

, while SIGTERM is sent to the scope's processes. The implementation still makes a best-effort Docker API call after signalling to look up a readable container name; its 3 s timeout can delay the next iteration. The important improvement is that Docker is no longer needed to deliver the kill:
Two other rules came out of failures:
On October 19, a llama.cpp server sat below 8 GiB while an older matcher looked only for vLLM. The matcher now includes

. If a hard or ramp kill is required and no eligible inference container matches, the fallback chooses the Docker scope with the largest sum of process RSS, provided that sum is at least 8 GiB. That fallback can kill an unrelated container, and summed RSS can double-count shared pages.
If a killed container has not disappeared 20 s later and memory is still below 3 GiB, the guard moves on to the next target instead of waiting.

An early version dropped caches 3 s after a kill, before a vLLM process that took about 10 s to exit had released its allocations. The current implementation normally waits for the scope's process list to empty, but it also proceeds after a 60 s timeout. A separate sweep runs every 5 s when non-slab
exceeds 8 GiB and the matcher finds no inference container. That scan does not prove the GPU is idle: native processes and other cgroup layouts are outside its view.
is system-wide and can cause extra I/O when useful cache must be rebuilt. I treat it as a targeted workaround to investigate, not routine memory housekeeping. The

and records whether it succeeded at startup. Its service uses

The published test summary reports an 82 GB over-commit run killed at 19.4 GiB of estimated headroom, a minimum of 18.8 GiB, and recovery in 4 s. A fresh SSH login was described as instant in an earlier version of that test, compared with about 50 s without the guard. A more severe 95 GB case bottomed at 3.6 GiB and recovered on its own. A 75 GB model then served for 4.1 hours at 12 to 21 GiB of headroom with no guard actions.

Those are observations from a small set of runs, not a reliability rate. The repository contains the implementation and result summaries, but not the complete raw traces needed to independently reconstruct these comparisons. A useful next result would repeat the same workloads with the current settings and publish the configuration, CSV, action log, and recovery measurement together.
The guard is the main intervention. The supporting settings aim to preserve access, improve logging, and provide recovery options if intervention is late.
This Ubuntu installation used socket activation for SSH.

influences the per-zone free-memory watermarks. I increased it from roughly 45 MB on this installation to 1 GiB, then reduced it to 256 MiB after examining the capacity cost. The original measurements suggested that the smaller setting returned about 1 GiB of headroom. It is not a separate, fixed-size emergency RAM pool, and the current setting still needs the same severe over-commit test used for the earlier one.
disables an additional reclaim boost triggered by fragmentation; ordinary reclaim still runs. This trades some proactive reclaim for retaining more cache during the observed loads.

The panic settings can turn a detected hung task or other configured kernel failure into a reboot; the hardware watchdog only works if a usable watchdog device exists and systemd stops servicing it. This is a recovery option, not a guarantee that every hang will reboot on a fixed schedule. I enable it for unattended benchmarks, accepting the loss of the interrupted run. See the

The installer enables persistent journaling with a 5 s sync interval and caps journal storage at 2 GB. This reduces the window of unsynced logs while the storage path is working; it cannot guarantee a final record during a stall.
disables the DGX Dashboard services, measured at about 380 MiB on this installation. It leaves
enabled. The earlier overhead estimate was about 0.2 GiB of extra kernel headroom plus 36 MiB for the daemons, but the larger capacity tradeoff is the guard's default 8 GiB soft threshold.
The server settings only help if the client does not give up first. With
drops the connection after 45 s without a reply, and with SSH multiplexing that takes the shared connection with it. A stall can last longer than that. I added:

body.code:
Host gx10
  ServerAliveInterval 15
  ServerAliveCountMax 12
  ControlMaster auto
  ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p
  ControlPersist 24h

The current 3 GiB hard floor and 256 MiB watermark setting have not been validated by the same 95 GB over-commit test. Until that comparison exists, the successful older runs should not be read as proof that the current defaults prevent the same failure.

The rate rule can stop a fast load that would have settled safely. At 17 GiB/s, the 0.5 s projection reaches a 3 GiB floor when current headroom is about 11.5 GiB; at 41 GiB/s it does so at about 23.5 GiB. A future guard could use expected allocation sizes, but knowing the planned KV-cache size alone would not account for every temporary allocation.
The default soft rule also stops a workload that stays below 8 GiB even if it appears stable.

makes that rule require measured memory pressure, but it does not change the hard or ramp rules. I have left it off while collecting a baseline. If PSI cannot be read, the implementation falls back to the plain soft rule.
suppresses signalling and the loop's cache drops, but the startup cleanup can still write to
. It is not a fully passive observation mode in this revision.

. It does not cover native servers, workloads inside VMs, rootless Docker, or Kubernetes/containerd scopes. With several matching containers, selection follows scope modification time, not per-workload GPU usage. The RSS fallback stays within those Docker scopes.

Driver and workload versions matter. In July, the OOM dump showed very little vLLM RSS; in October, with driver 595.99.02 instead of 595.71.05 and a newer vLLM, earlyoom saw a much larger process footprint. I have not isolated the cause, and the llama.cpp accounting difference remains unexplained.

The lesson from this box is to validate a memory signal against the workload and the host's ability to make progress. Record loading peaks, keep recovery access in mind, and separate measured results from tuning assumptions. If another GB10 system shows different accounting, a trace with the driver, kernel, and workload versions would make that comparison useful.

description: Why model loads made my GB10 host unresponsive, how a memory guard intervenes, and what the tests establish about its limits.
nextReadReason: Continue with GPU scheduling on the same hardware. Time-slicing adds scheduling slots; it does not provide memory isolation, and this Docker guard does not protect those pods.

takeaways: The GB10 shares memory between the CPU and GPU. In these incidents, model loading left the host unable to respond over SSH.
The guard intervenes against Docker workloads; it does not cover Kubernetes pods or every source of host memory pressure.
Successful tests used older thresholds. The current 3 GiB hard floor and 256 MiB min_free_kbytes defaults have not received the same validation.
